title: Learning From Failure: Integrating Negative Examples when Fine-tuning Large Language Models as Agents
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) used as agents can improve by learning not only from successful interaction trajectories but also from failed ones. Prior agent-tuning work typically keeps only successful trajectories when fine-tuning smaller models, discarding failed attempts as unusable. The authors argue that these negative examples contain useful information and ask two main questions: whether LLMs can learn from failed trajectories, and how such data should be incorporated to improve agent performance.

To address this, the paper proposes Negative-Aware Training (NAT), a fine-tuning approach in which both successful and unsuccessful trajectories are retained, but each is explicitly marked with prompts indicating whether the model should generate a correct or incorrect solution. The method is evaluated on agent-style tasks including mathematical reasoning, multi-hop question answering, and strategic question answering. Trajectories are generated with GPT-3.5 interacting with tools such as a calculator and search engine, then used to fine-tune LLaMA-2 chat models. The study compares NAT against two baselines: standard fine-tuning on positive trajectories only, and negative-unaware training that mixes positive and negative trajectories without labels.

The paper is not an education study with human learners; instead, the evaluated "population" is AI models on benchmark tasks. Therefore, no human participant group, classroom, or school context is reported. Experiments are conducted in an online computational environment using benchmark datasets such as GSM8K, HotpotQA, and StrategyQA. The work is relevant to AI in education mainly because it concerns improving reasoning-oriented AI systems that could potentially be used in educational settings.

The main conclusion is that negative trajectories can be useful during agent fine-tuning when the model is explicitly informed about their status. NAT generally outperforms training on positive examples alone and also outperforms naively mixing positive and negative examples. The authors further conclude that the quality of negative examples matters, that gains are especially notable in low-resource settings, and that NAT appears to improve reasoning/planning while reducing the harm caused by action errors relative to simple mixing. They also note limitations, including dependence on ground-truth labels and lack of experiments on more diverse or stronger models.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Large language models used as agents that reason, generate action trajectories, and interact with tools such as calculators and search engines; the paper studies a training paradigm for fine-tuning such LLM agents rather than a single commercial product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies negative-aware training (NAT) for fine-tuning LLaMA-2-based LLM agents using both successful and unsuccessful trajectories on math reasoning and question-answering tasks, with GPT-3.5 used to generate training trajectories.

findings.finding_summary: On math tasks, NAT improved average accuracy over positive-only fine-tuning across multiple LLaMA-2 settings. For LLaMA-2-7B with 2k positive examples, average accuracy increased from 55.90 (Vanilla) to 64.64 (NAT), an 8.74-point gain; with 5k positives, it increased from 64.17 to 67.42. For LLaMA-2-13B, average accuracy rose from 65.18 to 67.74 with 2k positives and from 70.76 to 71.28 with 5k positives.
findings.measure: Average accuracy across GSM8K, ASDiv, SVAMP, and MultiArith
findings.effect_size: 8.74 percentage-point gain (7B, 2k positives); 3.25 points (7B, 5k); 2.56 points (13B, 2k); 0.52 points (13B, 5k)

findings.finding_summary: On HotpotQA, NAT improved question answering performance over positive-only training, and a fine-grained variant (NAT-2) improved further. NAT-2 raised 7B performance from EM 27.44 / F1 36.41 (Vanilla) to EM 29.76 / F1 42.51, and 13B performance from EM 27.04 / F1 36.95 to EM 29.60 / F1 43.29; results were reported as mean scores over 5 runs.
findings.measure: Exact Match (EM) and F1 on HotpotQA
findings.sample_size: 5 runs; training examples described as 500 positive examples and up to 2k negative examples

findings.finding_summary: On StrategyQA, NAT outperformed both positive-only training and negative-unaware training. With 1000 positive samples and 500 negative samples, NAT achieved 65.80 on 7B versus 55.40 for Vanilla and 62.40 for NUT; on 13B, NAT achieved 64.60 versus 53.40 for Vanilla and 61.80 for NUT.
findings.effect_size: 7B: +10.40 points vs Vanilla, +3.40 vs NUT; 13B: +11.20 vs Vanilla, +2.80 vs NUT
findings.sample_size: training set: 1000 positive samples and 500 negative samples; evaluation n not_reported

findings.finding_summary: The quality of negative trajectories strongly affected outcomes. With LLaMA-2-7B and 10k negative samples, high-quality negatives improved average math accuracy from 55.90 to 64.64 in the 2k-positive setting and from 64.17 to 67.42 in the 5k-positive setting, whereas low-quality negatives reduced performance to 52.74 and 57.97 respectively.
findings.measure: Average accuracy across GSM8K, ASDiv, SVAMP, and MultiArith under different negative-data quality conditions
findings.effect_size: 2k positives: +8.74 with high-quality negatives vs -3.16 with low-quality negatives; 5k positives: +3.25 with high-quality negatives vs -6.20 with low-quality negatives

findings.finding_summary: In Chain-of-Thought fine-tuning on math tasks, NAT also improved performance relative to positive-only and negative-unaware training. Using LLaMA-2-7B with 2k positive samples and 1.6k negative samples, average accuracy increased from 52.69 (Vanilla) to 59.37 (NAT), compared with 58.45 for NUT.
findings.measure: Average accuracy across GSM8K, ASDiv, SVAMP, and MultiArith under CoT prompting
findings.effect_size: 6.68 percentage-point gain vs Vanilla; 0.92 vs NUT

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical AI-methods paper with benchmark evaluations, but it is not an education intervention study with student participants, randomized assignment, or classroom implementation. Evidence comes from task-performance experiments on datasets rather than K-12 learner outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported benchmark gains are often large in magnitude, including +8.74 percentage points on average math accuracy and roughly +6 F1 on HotpotQA. However, impacts are on benchmark task performance, not directly on student learning outcomes.
